plain: Docker is a sealed box where your program travels with everything it needs to run: the exact version of the language it's written in, its loose pieces, and its configuration. You don't install any of that on your computer: you install Docker and it opens the box. It's like getting a food truck's kitchen already assembled, with the oven, the wiring, and the burners fitted at the factory, instead of buying every appliance separately and praying they get along. That's why what works on your desk works exactly the same on the server: it's not that it resembles it, it's literally the same box.

account.free: The Personal plan is free and more than enough for the whole course: you download Docker Desktop, start whatever boxes you want, and pull public images without spending a dollar. The only downside of the free account is a per-hour download cap from the public catalog (Docker Hub); once you create the free account and sign in, that cap goes up and stops bothering you. The paid plans (Pro, Team, Business) run around 9, 15, and 24 dollars per person per month, but prices change and I'm not making them up: check them at docker.com/pricing before paying anything. You don't need them.
steps: Open docker.com. In the middle of the page there's a big blue button that says 'Download Docker Desktop'. Don't head to the 'Products' or 'Pricing' menus: the blue button is the spot.

Next to the button there's a small arrow that expands the options. On Windows choose 'Download for Windows - AMD64' unless your laptop is one of the newer ARM-processor ones (Snapdragon), in which case click 'ARM64'. On Mac you need to get right between 'Apple Silicon' (Macs from 2021 onward, with an M1, M2, M3, or M4 chip) and 'Intel Chip' (earlier ones); if you're not sure, click the apple icon top left, 'About This Mac', and read the 'Chip' line. It downloads a file between 600 MB and 1.5 GB (gigabytes, a few episodes' worth of a show). Two to ten minutes on fiber.

On Windows you get 'Docker Desktop Installer.exe'. Double-click it. A checked box shows up saying 'Use WSL 2 instead of Hyper-V (recommended)': leave it checked as is. It'll ask for your computer's administrator password (yours, the one that turns Windows on) and once it's done it'll force a restart. Save whatever you have open before clicking through. On Mac you download a .dmg, open it, and drag the whale icon into the 'Applications' folder.

The first time you open it, a window titled 'Docker Subscription Service Agreement' shows up with an 'Accept' button. There you're confirming your usage fits the free plan. If you work on your own or at a small company, it fits. Skim it before clicking.

Docker takes between 30 seconds and two minutes to start up the first time, and nothing works while it does. Look at the bottom-left corner of the window: there's a dot and some text. Once it says 'Engine running' and the dot is green, you can work. If it's orange and says 'Starting', wait.

Top right there's a 'Sign in' button. Click it, then 'Sign up', and create the account with your email. It's free and doesn't ask for a card. It's there so your downloads don't get cut off mid-afternoon. You can skip this today and do it the day you get the 'rate limit' error.

Open the Terminal (on Windows search 'Terminal' or 'PowerShell' in the start menu; on Mac it's in Applications, inside Utilities) and type: docker run hello-world . Press Enter. If after a few seconds a paragraph in English appears starting with 'Hello from Docker!', everything's fine and you can close it. If a red error shows up, check this guide's errors section.
account.warning: Two warnings, and both cost money or disk space. First, the license: Docker Desktop is free for you, for learning, and for small businesses, but stops being free if your company has more than 250 employees or makes more than 10 million dollars a year in revenue. Then a per-person license needs to be paid, and it's not you who signs it. If you work at a large company, ask before installing it on the work laptop. Second, disk space: Docker eats up space silently, without warning. Every box you try out leaves stuff saved behind, and after three weeks of the course that's 20, 30, or 50 GB gone without anyone telling you, until the computer starts complaining there's no room left. Get in the habit of typing 'docker system df' now and then to check.

first: Type in the Terminal: docker run hello-world . It's the litmus test. Installs nothing permanent, takes ten seconds, and tells you whether the install is fine before you lose an afternoon fighting something else.

Open Docker Desktop and click 'Containers' in the left menu. It's empty or nearly so. That's normal on day one and doesn't mean anything's wrong: that list is your control panel, and whatever you start is going to show up there.

Start a real website to see the magic. Type: docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name my-first-site nginx . Wait ten seconds and open localhost:8080 in your browser. You'll see a page that says 'Welcome to nginx!'. You just spun up a web server without installing any web server.

Now stop it from the interface. Go back to 'Containers', find the 'my-first-site' row, and click the stop square. Reload localhost:8080 in the browser: it no longer loads. Click the play triangle again: it loads again. That turning on and off is 80% of what you're going to do with Docker.

Delete it entirely with the trash icon on that same row and confirm. Then click the gear 'Settings' icon top right, go into 'Resources', and look at how much memory and disk you've handed over to it. If your computer has 16 GB, give it 6 or 8 at most and keep the rest for yourself.
shortcuts: The whale icon (Windows: bottom right next to the clock, maybe hidden behind the '^' arrow; Mac: top right, in the menu bar)

Tells you at a glance whether Docker is alive or asleep. Clicking it shows a short menu with 'Dashboard', 'Restart', and 'Quit Docker Desktop'. You'll check it every morning, because 90% of weird errors are simply that Docker isn't running.
The 'Containers' tab, first in the left menu

Your dashboard: what's on, on which port, since when, and how much memory it's using. Green with 'Running' means it's working; gray with 'Exited' means it's stopped or crashed. This is where any investigation of why something isn't working starts.
The play triangle and stop square, on each row

Turning on and off without typing a single command. Play starts the box exactly as it was; stop turns it off without deleting it, so you can turn it back on tomorrow with everything still inside. It's the equivalent of a lamp switch.
The blue port link, like '8080:80', on the container's row
Click it and your browser opens straight into your application, without you having to remember the number. When the AI says 'open localhost:whatever', this link saves you the guessing.
Clicking the container's name and then the 'Logs' tab

The diary of what your program is saying on the inside. When something fails, the explanation is here, almost always in the last ten lines and in red. It's the place you'll spend the most time, and the one that'll save you the most grief.
The 'Exec' tab, inside the container

Puts a command window inside the box, as if you were sitting at the computer inside it. Useful for checking if a file is where it should be. Only use it when the AI asks you to and tells you exactly what to type.
The 'Images' tab in the left menu, with its 'Size' column

The warehouse of downloaded molds and how much space each one takes. Sort by size by clicking the column header and you'll see at a glance what's eating your disk. Delete by checking the box and clicking the trash can.
Ctrl+K on Windows / Cmd+K on Mac

Opens Docker Desktop's quick search to find a container or an image by name without going tab by tab. Works in recent versions; if it does nothing in yours, use the magnifying glass in the top bar, which does the same thing.
The bug icon top right, and inside it 'Restart Docker Desktop'

The official off-and-on-again. When Docker gets stuck (unresponsive, the whale stays orange forever, commands hang), this fixes it more often than it's comfortable to admit. Doesn't delete anything of yours.
The gear 'Settings' → 'Resources'

This is where you decide how much memory and how many cores your computer lends Docker. If the laptop struggles and the fan roars while you work, lower the memory here. It's the difference between Docker being a polite tenant and one who takes over your living room.
daily: Go into your project's folder and type: docker compose up -d . Starts your whole project (the site, the database, whatever's there) at once and hands you back a free Terminal. The '-d' means it keeps running in the background and you can carry on with other things.

Type: docker compose logs -f . This is watching, live, what your program is saying while it runs, line by line. When something doesn't load in the browser, this command tells you why 90% of the time. Exit with Ctrl+C, which breaks nothing.

Type: docker compose down . Turns off and tidies away the whole project. Data saved in volumes survives; what gets swept away are the boxes, which get recreated identical tomorrow. It's the clean way to end the day.

Type: docker compose up -d --build . This is what you need to use every time the AI changes your code. Without '--build', Docker reuses the old box and you go crazy wondering why your changes aren't showing up. Write this down: it's the number one mistake beginners make.

Type: docker ps . The list of what's currently running, with its name and port. Two seconds of typing this saves you ten minutes of guessing. If it comes back empty, nothing's running, and that's the end of the mystery.

Type: docker system df . Tells you in gigabytes how much Docker is taking up on your disk, split between images, containers, and volumes. Check it once a week. It's the only way to find out your computer is filling up before it becomes a problem.
Restart Docker Desktop from the bug icon when something behaves inexplicably. Before investigating for half an hour, try this: it takes a minute and resolves an indecent number of phantom failures.

templates.name: Complete project with a database, start and stop with one command
templates.what: A docker-compose.yml file (the file that describes every piece of your project and how they talk to each other) for a web application with a PostgreSQL database. Works for any project the AI writes for you that needs to save things: a shop, a customer dashboard, an assistant with memory. Data is stored in a named volume, so you can delete and recreate the box a thousand times without losing it.
templates.how: 1) Create a file named exactly docker-compose.yml in your project's main folder, the same one that has the Dockerfile. 2) Paste the content below. 3) Create another file next to it called .env (with the dot in front) and put your private keys there, one per line, in the format NAME=value. 4) Change the three things in the fill-in table. 5) Open the Terminal in that folder and type: docker compose up -d . 6) Wait about a minute the first time, because it's downloading the database. 7) Open localhost:3000 in the browser. 8) To shut everything down: docker compose down .
fill: CHANGE_THIS_KEY (appears twice, and both must be identical)
A password you make up for the database. Any long, space-free string works, like 'blue-melon-1978'. It's local, nobody else sees it, but change it anyway.
The door number you open your app with in the browser. If you get a port-already-in-use error, put 3001 on the left one and leave the right one as is. Then open localhost:3001.
The name of your database and its user. If you have no preference, leave it as is: works the same and avoids confusion.
Your real private keys: your OpenAI API key, your Stripe key, whatever it is. Never write these inside the docker-compose.yml or the Dockerfile.
templates.code:
# docker-compose.yml
# Goes in your project's main folder, next to the Dockerfile.

services:

  web:
    build: .
    container_name: my-app-web
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    env_file:
      - .env
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://myuser:CHANGE_THIS_KEY@database:5432/mydb
      NODE_ENV: production
    depends_on:
      database:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  database:
    image: postgres:16
    container_name: my-app-db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: myuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: CHANGE_THIS_KEY
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U myuser -d mydb"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  postgres-data:

templates.name: The box for a web app the AI wrote for you (Node)
templates.what: A Dockerfile (the written recipe for how your box gets built) and its .dockerignore (the list of what must NOT go into the box), for this course's most common case: the AI wrote you a Node web application and you want to put it into Docker. The .dockerignore isn't optional extra: it's what stops your passwords from ending up inside the image and traveling with you to the server.
templates.how: 1) Create a file in your project's main folder named exactly Dockerfile, no dot and no extension. Paste the first part of the code. 2) Create another named exactly .dockerignore, dot in front, no extension. Paste the second part. 3) Check what your application's startup file is called: the AI usually names it server.js, index.js, or app.js. Change the last line of the Dockerfile if yours is named differently. 4) In the Terminal, inside that folder: docker build -t my-app . (watch the trailing dot, it's part of the command). 5) Start it: docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env --name my-app my-app . 6) Open localhost:3000 . If it doesn't load, check the logs.
fill: The real name of the file that starts your application. If you don't know, ask the AI: 'tell me which file starts my application'.
The 3000 in EXPOSE and in PORT
The port your app listens on. If the AI wrote it for 8000 or 5000, change both numbers here and also in the start command.
The Node version your project needs. If the AI tells you it uses 20, put node:20-slim. If you have no idea, leave it at 22.
templates.code:
# ============ FILE 1: Dockerfile ============

FROM node:22-slim

WORKDIR /app

# First just the list of pieces: this way Docker doesn't
# re-download them every time you touch a line of your code.
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --omit=dev

# Now, the rest of the project.
COPY . .

ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV PORT=3000
EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "server.js"]


# ============ FILE 2: .dockerignore ============
# Everything listed here does NOT go into the box.
# The .env line is the most important one on either list.

node_modules
npm-debug.log
.env
.env.*
.git
.gitignore
.vscode
.idea
dist
build
coverage
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
*.md
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

templates.name: Panic button: reclaim space without wrecking your data
templates.what: The exact sequence, in order and with a safety net, for when Docker has eaten your disk or everything is behaving strangely and you want to start fresh. It's designed so you look before you delete, and so you never touch volumes by accident, which is where the things you can't recover live.
templates.how: Run the commands one at a time, in the order given, reading the output before moving to the next. Don't paste them all at once. 1 and 4 only look, they delete nothing. 3 deletes but is safe: it doesn't touch your data. 5 is the dangerous one and is kept separate on purpose: only use it if you know exactly which volume you're deleting and why. If you have a project with docker-compose.yml, instead of command 2 you can go into its folder and type: docker compose down .
fill: The exact name that showed up in 'docker volume ls'. Copy and paste it, don't type it from memory: get the volume wrong and you delete the wrong data.
templates.code:
# 1. LOOK first. This command deletes nothing.
#    Tells you in gigabytes what each thing takes up and how much is
#    "reclaimable", i.e. junk you can throw away without worry.
docker system df


# 2. Stop everything that's running. Deletes nothing.
#    If nothing's running it'll show a warning: harmless.
docker stop $(docker ps -q)


# 3. SAFE CLEANUP. Deletes stopped containers, dangling networks,
#    images nobody's using anymore, and build caches.
#    Does NOT touch volumes, meaning it does NOT touch your data.
#    It'll ask you to confirm by typing y. Usually frees 5 to 40 GB.
docker system prune -a


# 4. See what volumes you have and how much space they take. Look-only.
docker volume ls
docker system df -v


# 5. DANGER. This DELETES THAT VOLUME'S DATA FOREVER.
#    No trash can, no undo, no backup.
#    Only if you're sure that volume belongs to a test project
#    you no longer care about.
docker volume rm volume-name

errors: error during connect: Head "http://%2F%2F.%2Fpipe%2FdockerDesktopLinuxEngine/_ping": open //./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine: The system cannot find the file specified.  (on Mac it shows as: Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock. Is the docker daemon running?)

The most common error of all and the silliest: Docker Desktop isn't running. Doesn't matter what you type, there's nobody on the other end listening. Open Docker Desktop from the start menu or from Applications, wait for the bottom-left corner to say 'Engine running' with the green dot, and repeat the command. If Docker is open and this still shows up, restart it via the bug icon → 'Restart Docker Desktop'.
Error response from daemon: Ports are not available: exposing port TCP 0.0.0.0:3000 -> 0.0.0.0:0: listen tcp 0.0.0.0:3000: bind: address already in use

That door number is already being used by something else: another box you left running yesterday, or a normal application on your computer. The one-second fix is to change the LEFT number in your docker-compose.yml or start command: put "3001:3000" instead of "3000:3000", then open localhost:3001 in the browser. Never touch the right one, because that's the port inside the box, and your program expects that one. If you'd rather free up 3000, type 'docker ps' to see who has it and stop it from Docker Desktop.
Error response from daemon: pull access denied for my-app, repository does not exist or may require 'docker login': denied: requested access to the resource is denied

Docker went looking for a prefab box in the public catalog and it doesn't exist under that name. Almost always a typo in the image name (postgress with two s's instead of postgres, node:22-slimm) or the AI made up an image name that doesn't exist. Copy the whole error to the AI and ask it to confirm the exact name and version tag. This also happens if your project has its own Dockerfile but you put 'image:' in the docker-compose.yml instead of 'build: .'.
toomanyrequests: You have reached your pull rate limit. You may increase the limit by authenticating and upgrading: https://www.docker.com/increase-rate-limit

You've pulled too many boxes in a few hours without signing in. The public catalog limits anonymous downloads. It's not your fault and it costs nothing to fix: create the free account at hub.docker.com, then in the Terminal type 'docker login', enter your username and password, and try again. You can also sign in from the 'Sign in' button in Docker Desktop, which is the same thing. If you're in a hurry and don't want to sign up, wait a few hours and try again.
write /var/lib/docker/overlay2/...: no space left on device

There's no room left on the disk Docker uses. Note: this can happen even with your computer's disk half-empty, because on Windows and Mac Docker lives in its own space with its own cap. First look: 'docker system df'. Then the safe cleanup: 'docker system prune -a', which will ask you to confirm with the letter y and usually frees 5 to 40 GB without touching your data. If that's still not enough, go into Settings → Resources and raise Docker's disk limit.
Your container shows up gray in Docker Desktop with the text: Exited (1) 3 seconds ago

Your program started inside the box, crashed, and shut itself down. The box is fine; what's failing is the code inside it. The cause is NOT in that message, it's in the logs: click the container's name and then the 'Logs' tab, or type in the Terminal 'docker compose logs --tail 50'. Read the last few lines, copy them in full, and hand them to the AI. The three typical causes are: a missing variable in the .env file, the database wasn't ready yet, or the Dockerfile's startup file name doesn't match the real one.

The box is built for a different type of processor than your computer's. This mostly happens on Macs with an M1, M2, M3, or M4 chip when you try to use an image built only for Intel, and also the other way around. Add --platform linux/amd64 to the start command, or the line 'platform: linux/amd64' below the service name in the docker-compose.yml. It'll work, but noticeably slower because your Mac is translating on the fly. If you can, ask the AI for an image that has an ARM version.
Docker Desktop requires a newer WSL kernel version.  /  Hardware assisted virtualization and data execution protection must be enabled in the BIOS

Windows only, and only on day one. The first message is fixed by opening PowerShell as administrator (right-click the start menu → 'Terminal (Admin)') and typing: wsl --update . Then restart the computer. The second is more uncomfortable: virtualization is turned off in your motherboard's BIOS, the menu you get into by pressing F2, F10, or Delete right after turning the computer on. There you need to enable the option called 'Intel VT-x', 'SVM Mode', or 'Virtualization'. If touching the BIOS makes you nervous, that's entirely reasonable: ask someone for help before changing anything in there.

prompts.name: Put your project into Docker from scratch, without knowing how to code
prompts.prompt: You're my Docker expert and I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn: tell me exactly what to type and where, don't assume anything. I want to put my project into Docker so it always starts the same way and doesn't break when I switch computers or upload it to a server. My project is [DESCRIBE YOUR PROJECT IN ONE SENTENCE: for example, an online shop that stores orders in a database]. The files are in the folder [FULL PATH TO YOUR FOLDER]. I work on [WINDOWS 11 OR MACOS] and I have Docker Desktop installed with the whale green. Before writing anything, look at my project's files and tell me in four lines what you found: what language it's in, what command starts it today, what port it listens on, and whether it needs a database. Then write me three complete, ready-to-paste files, each in its own block, telling me the exact name it should have and which folder it goes in: the Dockerfile, the docker-compose.yml, and the .dockerignore. Rules you can't skip: no passwords or API keys inside the Dockerfile or the image, all of that goes in a .env file that must be listed in the .dockerignore; if there's a database, use a named volume so the data survives deleting the container; and use specific image versions, no 'latest'. When you're done, give me the exact list of commands I need to type in the Terminal, in order, one per line, with a sentence explaining what each one does, which browser address I need to check to confirm it's working, and exactly what I should see on screen if it went well.

prompts.name: Translate a Docker error and fix it
prompts.prompt: I'm not a programmer and I'm using Docker Desktop on [WINDOWS 11 OR MACOS]. I typed this command in the Terminal: [PASTE THE EXACT COMMAND YOU TYPED] and got this error, copied exactly, in full, without removing a single line: [PASTE THE COMPLETE ERROR HERE]. My project is [DESCRIBE YOUR PROJECT IN ONE SENTENCE] and it's in the folder [YOUR FOLDER'S PATH]. Explain it in plain English, no jargon, and answer these four questions separately and in this order: what that error means in plain terms; what the most likely cause is in my specific case, not in general; what's happening right now inside my computer; and whether I've lost any data or if everything's still there. Then give me the fix as complete copy-paste-ready commands, one per line, in the exact order I need to type them, with a sentence under each saying what it does. If any of those commands deletes something irreversibly, warn me BEFORE it in capital letters and tell me exactly what's lost and whether there's a way to recover it. If there are two ways to fix it, a quick provisional one and a proper one, give me both and tell me which suits me if I'm just learning and not in a hurry. And end by telling me what I need to do differently next time so this doesn't happen again, in a single sentence I can write down.

prompts.name: The container starts and shuts itself down
prompts.prompt: I have a Docker container that starts and dies within a few seconds. In Docker Desktop, in the 'Containers' tab, it shows up gray and says [COPY THE EXACT TEXT OF THAT ROW HERE, FOR EXAMPLE: Exited (1) 5 seconds ago]. I don't know how to code, so I need you to guide me. These are the complete logs from typing docker compose logs --tail 100, pasted without trimming: [PASTE ALL THE LOG LINES HERE]. My docker-compose.yml is this: [PASTE THE FILE'S CONTENTS HERE]. And my Dockerfile is this: [PASTE THE FILE'S CONTENTS HERE]. Start by pointing me to the specific line in the logs where the real problem is, because I can't tell what matters from what's normal noise. Tell me in one sentence what's failing. Then give me the three most likely hypotheses, ranked from most to least likely, and for each one a quick check I can do with a single command or by looking at a specific Docker Desktop screen, to rule it in or out. Once you're sure of the cause, give me the corrected files in full, not fragments or patches, because I don't know how to paste a piece into the middle of a file without breaking it. And explain at the end whether the problem was in the code, in Docker's configuration, or in one piece starting before another, because I want to learn to tell those apart.

prompts.name: Space audit: what can I delete without losing anything
prompts.prompt: Docker is filling up my hard drive and I don't know what I can delete without wrecking something important. I'm not a programmer, so treat me as if every command you give me could break something. This is the result of typing docker system df -v in my Terminal, pasted in full: [PASTE THE FULL RESULT HERE]. And this is what shows up when typing docker ps -a: [PASTE THE FULL RESULT HERE]. The projects I do care about and don't want to lose are: [NAME YOUR PROJECTS, FOR EXAMPLE: my-shop and the customer assistant]. Everything else is old testing I no longer use. Make me a table with three columns: what each thing on the list is in plain language, how much space it takes, and whether it's safe to delete, questionable, or untouchable. Mark as untouchable anything containing data that can't be recovered, especially database volumes, and tell me which project each one belongs to so I can decide. Then give me the cleanup commands in two clearly separated blocks: first the SAFE block, the one I can run with my eyes closed without losing any data, with an estimate of how many gigabytes I'll recover; then the DANGEROUS block, one command per line, each with a warning in capital letters of exactly what's lost and that there's no trash can or way to undo it. Do not mix the two blocks under any circumstances.

prompts.name: Explain my docker-compose.yml line by line
prompts.prompt: This is my project's docker-compose.yml file, which you wrote for me and I don't understand: [PASTE THE COMPLETE FILE CONTENT HERE]. My project is [DESCRIBE YOUR PROJECT IN ONE SENTENCE]. I don't know how to code and I don't want to learn how to write these files, but I do want to understand what's in front of me so I don't break it every time I touch something. Explain it like this: first, in five lines with a real-life comparison, what this file does as a whole and what pieces it's assembling. Second, go block by block, and for each one tell me what it's for, in one sentence, without a single technical word you don't translate in parentheses the first time you write it. Third, and this is what matters most to me, give me two clear lists: the list of lines I CAN safely change and exactly what happens if I change each one, and the list of lines I must NEVER touch, with an explanation of what breaks if I do. Fourth, tell me if you see anything wrong, anything dangerous, or anything that's going to fall apart once this leaves my computer: passwords written in plain sight, data that wouldn't survive a deletion, open ports that shouldn't be, or unpinned versions. And finish with the four commands I'll use 95% of the days with this file, each with a sentence on when it's used.

words: Image

The frozen mold. It's a large, read-only file containing your program and everything it needs. It doesn't run: it's saved, copied, and shipped. Think of a movie's master copy: nobody watches the master, copies are made from it.
Container

The live copy of the mold, already turned on and running. From the same image you can launch twenty identical containers. It's what you start, stop, and delete every day. And importantly: when you delete it, it takes everything inside it that wasn't in a volume with it.
Dockerfile

The written recipe, in a text file with no extension named exactly that. It says what base you're starting from, what gets copied in, what gets installed, and what command starts the program. It's the only file that turns your project into an image.
Volume

A separate drawer that Docker keeps outside the box and that survives deleting the container. It's where things that can't be lost need to live: the database, files your users upload. Whatever's inside the box and not in a volume disappears without warning.
Port

A door number. When you write 3000:3000, the left one is your computer's door, the one you type into the browser; the right one is the door inside the box, decided by the program. Changing the left one is harmless; changing the right one breaks things.
docker compose

The orchestra conductor. One single file, docker-compose.yml, describes every piece of your project (the site, the database, the search engine) and how they talk to each other. One command starts them all, another stops them all. Without it you'd have to start each one by hand.
Docker Hub

The public catalog of ready-made molds, at hub.docker.com. It has databases, web servers, and languages, free and ready to download. When you write 'image: postgres:16', Docker goes there to find it. With a free account you can pull more per hour than without one.
Engine (daemon)

The program that actually does the work, always running in the background with no window of its own. Docker Desktop is just the remote control; the engine is the TV. When something 'can't connect to Docker', it's almost always the engine being off.
Logs

The diary of what your program says while it runs: what starts, what it finds, what hurts. It's raw, ugly text, and it always holds the explanation of why something's failing, usually in the last few lines. The place to ALWAYS check before assuming anything.
Build

Cooking the image from the recipe. Docker reads the Dockerfile, works through each step, and leaves the mold ready. The first time it takes minutes because everything gets downloaded; the following times it takes seconds because it reuses what it already did. You need to rebuild every time your code changes.
matters: Data only survives if it's in a volume, and this doesn't forgive mistakes. A container is disposable: anything written inside it and not in a volume vanishes the moment you delete it, no trash can, no warning, no way to recover it. The specific trap that catches almost everyone is the command 'docker compose down -v': it looks like the shut-down one, but that '-v' means also delete the volumes, meaning your entire database. Learn the difference: 'docker compose down' shuts off and keeps; 'docker compose down -v' shuts off and destroys. And if the project is getting serious, volume or no volume, keep separate database backups: Docker stores your data, it doesn't protect it.

Changes the AI makes don't get into the box on their own. You ask the AI to fix something, it rewrites the code, you reload the browser, and nothing's changed. And that's when an hour gets lost arguing with the AI about a problem that doesn't exist. What's happening is that Docker is still using the box built before your changes. The right command after every code change is 'docker compose up -d --build': that '--build' recooks the image with the new stuff. If you're working without compose, it's 'docker build -t my-app .' and then restarting. It hurts to ignore this because it throws no error: everything just stays the same and you go crazy.

Keys and passwords never go inside the image. An image isn't a secret: it gets copied, uploaded to a server, and anyone who has it can open it and read what's inside, including the lines you thought were private. Write your OpenAI or Stripe API key inside the Dockerfile and it's in there forever, and deleting the line afterward doesn't remove it from earlier layers. Keys go in a .env file, and .env goes listed in the .dockerignore so it never gets in. This isn't purism: a leaked API key gets found by automated bots within minutes and spent. Bills of hundreds or thousands of dollars from an accidentally published key happen every week.

Docker grows on your disk silently, and only you can stop it. Every time you rebuild an image, the old one doesn't get deleted: it sits there, orphaned, taking up space. Every box you tried out on a Tuesday stays saved. In a normal course that's 20, 30, or 50 GB in a few weeks, and the warning doesn't come until the whole computer starts failing from lack of space, which is the worst possible moment. The habit that saves you costs ten seconds a week: type 'docker system df', look at the 'reclaimable' column, and if there are a lot of gigabytes there, run 'docker system prune -a', which deletes the junk without touching your volumes.
ignore: Optimizing image size: multi-stage builds, alpine images, counting layers, shrinking from 900 MB to 80 MB. It's a whole sport with its own championships. While you're learning, a fat image works exactly the same as a slim one: it just takes a bit longer to build and takes up more disk. Come back to this the day you're paying for the server.

Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, orchestration, replicas, autoscaling. All of that solves the problem of having hundreds of boxes spread across dozens of machines serving millions of people. You have two boxes on a laptop. Diving in there now is learning to direct air traffic to go to the grocery store.

Creating networks by hand with 'docker network create', configuring bridges, subnets, and internal addresses. Docker Compose already creates a private network for your project and makes the pieces find each other by name. That works on its own and covers absolutely everything you'll do this year.
